name: Write to you, not the user

source.section: Talking to the reader > Write to you
source.quote: Address that person as you. Don't write the user.

message: The guide addresses the reader directly as "you". "The user" puts a third person between the product and the reader.
fix: Rewrite to "you" ("You get an email when someone assigns you a task"). Use "user" only as a category word, such as "user permissions", or in developer documentation where it means the end user of the reader's software.

flag: The user receives an email when a task is assigned.
After the user saves the change, the dialog closes.
pass: You get an email when someone assigns you a task.
Open the user account page to change user permissions.
The end user of your app sees the error.

name: Don't use we to give advice

source.section: Talking to the reader > Use we only when the company is speaking
source.quote: Don't use we to give advice. "We recommend that you back up your data" becomes "Back up your data."

message: Advice phrased as a wish or as the company's opinion is longer and softer than a command. The guide reserves "we" for times when the company must be the speaker, such as a privacy notice or an outage update.
fix: Give the instruction as a command: "Back up the database before you upgrade."

flag: We recommend that you back up your data.
It is recommended that you consider backing up the database.
pass: Back up your data.
We encrypt your files at rest and in transit.

name: No first person singular in documentation

source.section: Talking to the reader > I, me, and my
source.quote: In documentation, never use first person singular.

message: Documentation speaks to the reader, not from a narrator. First person singular is allowed only in UI text where the reader is the speaker ("Keep me signed in") or in a product persona's own messages.
fix: Rewrite as a statement about the product or as a command to the reader.

flag: I recommend that you restart the connector first.
pass: Restart the connector first.
Select Keep me signed in.

name: Cut "you can" when the sentence works without it

source.section: Talking to the reader > Write to you
source.quote: Cut you can when the sentence works without it.

message: A sentence that starts with "you can" is often a plain instruction in disguise. The guide's example turns "You can export the report as a CSV file" into "Export the report as a CSV file."
fix: Try the sentence as a command. "You can" is right when it marks a choice rather than an instruction.

flag: You can export the report as a CSV file.
pass: Export the report as a CSV file.
You can only export your own reports.

name: Cut words, not facts

source.quote: Long phrases that mean the same as a short one are the easiest cut.

terms.match: in spite of the fact that

message: This phrase means the same as a shorter one. Every word should do work.
fix: Use the short form from the guide's table.

flag: Back up the database prior to the upgrade.
The system provides the ability to filter tasks by due date.
Use the filter in order to narrow the list.
pass: Back up the database before the upgrade.
Filter tasks by due date.

name: "A number of" hides the number

source.quote: a number of | several, or the number

message: "A number of" is vague. If the count is known, give it. Otherwise "several" is shorter.
fix: Write the actual number, or "several".

flag: A number of tasks are overdue.
pass: Several tasks are overdue.
The number of overdue tasks is shown in red.

name: Choose plain words

source.quote: use | utilize, leverage. help | facilitate, empower. through, by, using | via.

message: The guide prefers the short, common word. "Enable" stays when it means turn on.
fix: Replace with the plain word. For "via", choose "through", "by", or "using" to fit the sentence.

flag: Utilize the filter to narrow the list.
Send the report via email.
This feature empowers teams to leverage their data.
pass: Use the filter to narrow the list.
Send the report by email.
Enable the setting to turn on notifications.

name: Sign in, not log in

source.quote: sign in (verb), sign-in (noun) | log in, login | House style

message: House style uses "sign in" as the verb and "sign-in" as the noun. A swap that would rename an existing UI label everywhere is a product decision, so flag that case rather than changing one screen.
fix: Use "sign in" for the action and "sign-in" for the noun or adjective.

flag: Log in to see your tasks.
The login page shows an error.
pass: Sign in to see your tasks.
The sign-in page shows an error.

name: Set up is the verb, setup is the noun

source.quote: set up (verb), setup (noun) | setup (as a verb) | The verb is two words

message: "Setup" is written as one word only as a noun. As a verb it is two words.
fix: Write "set up" when it is something the reader does.

flag: First, setup the connector.
You need to setup a project.
pass: First, set up the connector.
The setup takes five minutes.
Read the welcome screen and setup overview.

name: Email, not e-mail

source.quote: email | e-mail | Current spelling

message: The guide spells it as one word with no hyphen.
fix: Write "email".

flag: Send an e-mail to the admin.
pass: Send an email to the admin.

name: Dialog, not dialog box or pop-up

source.quote: dialog | dialog box, pop-up | Shortest clear term

message: The guide uses the shortest clear term for a dialog.
fix: Write "dialog".

flag: A dialog box opens.
A pop-up asks you to confirm.
pass: A dialog opens.

name: Checkbox, not check box

source.quote: checkbox | check box | Current spelling

message: The guide spells it as one word.
fix: Write "checkbox".

flag: Clear the check box.
pass: Clear the checkbox.

name: Select, not click or tap

source.quote: Avoid click and tap. Each assumes one input device.

message: "Select" works for every input method. Keys are still pressed.
fix: Use "select" for options, values, links, menu items, and buttons.

flag: Click the Save button.
Tap Done to finish.
pass: Select Save.
Press Enter to finish.

name: Clear a checkbox, don't uncheck it

source.quote: Clear | Unchecking a checkbox

message: The guide's interaction verb for clearing a checkbox is "clear". Selecting one is "select".
fix: Write "Clear the ... checkbox."

flag: Uncheck the Send email notifications box.
pass: Clear the Send email notifications checkbox.

name: Cyberattack and cyberthreat are one word

source.quote: cyberattack, cyberthreat | cyber attack, cyber-attack | One word

message: The guide writes these as one word.
fix: Write "cyberattack" or "cyberthreat".

flag: Protect against a cyber attack.
pass: Protect against a cyberattack.

name: Avoid Latin abbreviations

source.quote: Avoid Latin abbreviations. Write for example, that is, and and so on. Readers and translation tools misread e.g., i.e., and etc.

message: Readers and translation tools misread Latin abbreviations.
fix: Write "for example", "that is", or name the items. For "etc.", prefer "such as" before the list, or say what is included.

flag: Supported formats, e.g. CSV and PDF.
Export tasks, comments, etc.
pass: Supported formats, for example CSV and PDF.
Export items such as tasks and comments.

name: Filler intensifiers

source.quote: (delete) | very, really, quite, rather, actually, basically, simply, just, easily, truly, genuinely, literally | Filler intensifiers

message: These words add emphasis but no fact. Inside a quotation or a product name they stay.
fix: Delete the word, unless the sentence then loses a fact.

flag: The backlog was very quickly cleared out.
This is actually the default.
pass: The backlog cleared.
This is the default.

name: Just, simply, and rather as filler

source.quote: Delete a word from the delete rows only when it's working as an intensifier. Just meaning "only" or "a moment ago" ... stay.

message: Often filler, but not always. "Just" meaning "only" or "a moment ago" stays. "Rather than" is not an intensifier.
fix: Delete it if the sentence means the same without it.

flag: Simply select Save to finish.
It's just a quick setting.
pass: Select Save to finish.
Use a list rather than a table.

name: Marketing words that carry no fact

source.quote: (delete) | seamlessly, robust, powerful, intuitive, cutting-edge, best-in-class, world-class | Marketing words that carry no fact

message: This word makes a claim without a fact behind it. Say what the product does instead.
fix: Delete it, or replace it with a concrete statement of behavior.

flag: A powerful, intuitive dashboard that integrates seamlessly.
This release brings blazing-fast uploads and a brand-new viewer.
pass: The dashboard refreshes every 5 minutes.

name: Products don't think

source.quote: A model ranks, selects, estimates, predicts, and recommends. It doesn't understand, believe, or know.

message: This gives the product a mind. The guide treats it as a claim for the author to confirm, not a style edit.
fix: Flag it for the author and suggest a verb such as ranks, selects, estimates, predicts, or recommends.

flag: The assistant understands what you mean.
pass: The assistant matches your question to related help articles.

name: Don't promise outcomes

source.section: Writing about product behavior > Don't promise outcomes
source.quote: Avoid always, never, guarantees, ensures, and eliminates when you describe what a model does.

message: An unqualified promise is one the product can't keep, because results depend on the customer's data and configuration. This is a claim for the author, not a style edit.
fix: Flag it. Suggest a plain statement of what the product does, or a verb such as ranks, selects, estimates, predicts, or recommends.

flag: Recommendations guarantee higher customer satisfaction.
The AI always picks the best answer.
pass: Recommendations rank the articles most likely to answer the question.

name: One generic term for the AI feature

source.quote: pick AI assistant or virtual assistant and don't alternate among assistant, bot, chatbot, and agent in one document.

message: This document uses more than one generic term for the same capability. Readers take different words for different things, and "agent" can also mean a person.
fix: Pick one generic term, such as "AI assistant", and use it throughout.

flag: The chatbot answers questions. The bot also files tasks.
pass: The AI assistant answers questions. The AI assistant also files tasks.

name: Don't use a brand as a verb

source.quote: Don't use a brand as a verb or a common noun. "Slack me" becomes "Send me a message in Slack."

message: A brand name is a proper noun, not a verb.
fix: Name the action and the product: "Send me a message in Slack."

flag: Slack me when the build finishes.
pass: Send me a message in Slack when the build finishes.

name: Use the owner's exact casing for brand names

source.quote: Use the owner's exact casing everywhere.

message: The brand table in the guide gives the owner's casing. Only the brands the guide itself prints are checked. Add your own rows to this rule when you fill in the brand table.
fix: Use the casing from the brand table.

flag: Connect your Github account.
Open the app on MacOS.
pass: Connect your GitHub account.
Open the app on macOS.

name: Technology terms are common nouns

source.section: Capitalization > Proper nouns and common nouns
source.quote: Most technology terms are common nouns, so they're lowercase: cloud computing, machine learning, open source, single sign-on.

message: A feature or a technology is a common noun unless it has a branded name. When you're editing someone else's text, flag it rather than changing the case.
fix: Lowercase the term unless it is part of a product name.

flag: The report uses Machine Learning to rank tasks.
pass: The report uses machine learning to rank tasks.
Machine learning ranks the tasks.

name: File formats in capitals

source.quote: File formats: The format in capitals, the extension in code style. Export a CSV file. The file ends in `.csv`.

message: In prose, write the format name in capitals. An extension such as .csv belongs in code style.
fix: Capitalize the format name, or put the extension in code style.

flag: Export a csv file.
pass: Export a CSV file.
The file ends in `.csv`.
